description: Deliberately bad inputs, each declaring its required outcome. How an implementation handles rubbish is part of the protocol: an implementation that accepts everything looks perfectly healthy right up until something malformed reaches it. Outcomes are 'reject' (refuse and say so), 'ignore' (drop silently, no error) and 'accept' (decode successfully; the input is unusual but legal). The ignore/reject split is not cosmetic — see unknown_message_type.

cases.name: bad_magic
cases.description: First byte is not 0x4C. Almost always another protocol on a shared port rather than corruption, which is why it is worth a cheap check before anything else happens.

cases.name: unsupported_major_version
cases.description: Major version 1. Majors are not forward compatible by construction, so this is a rejection and not an ignore: the sender needs to know.

cases.name: higher_minor_version_is_accepted
cases.description: Minor version 9 from a peer ahead of us. This MUST parse. Together with the unknown-type rule below it is the whole forward-compatibility story: a newer peer may add message types and fields, and an older one keeps talking to it.

cases.name: unknown_message_type
cases.description: Type 0x99 is not assigned. The required outcome is IGNORE, not reject. This is the rule that makes minor-version additions safe: an implementation that rejects here turns every future message type into a compatibility break, and it will look perfectly healthy until the day someone ships one.
cases.reason: unassigned type codes are dropped silently

cases.name: vendor_message_type
cases.description: Type 0xF5 is in the vendor range the spec will never assign. Ignored exactly like any other unknown type — a receiver has no way to tell 'not mine' from 'not yet invented' and must not try.

cases.name: payload_len_over_declares
cases.description: payload_len says 9, eight bytes are present. Trusting the declared length here is how a decoder reads into the AEAD tag.

cases.name: payload_len_under_declares
cases.description: payload_len says 7, eight bytes are present. The mirror case, and the one an implementation is more likely to wave through because nothing overruns.

cases.name: truncated_mid_header
cases.description: Twelve bytes: the datagram ends inside the header.

cases.name: truncated_before_tag
cases.description: Header and payload complete, tag missing. Every datagram costs 40 bytes of overhead and a receiver may not assume the tag is optional.

cases.name: declared_empty_payload_for_a_type_that_needs_one
cases.description: A well-formed 40-byte envelope declaring payload_len 0 for a SYNC_REQ, which needs eight. Framing succeeds and the payload decode is what must fail — an implementation that only validates the envelope passes this and then reads uninitialised memory for t1.
cases.reason: SYNC_REQ needs 8 payload bytes and none are present

cases.name: empty_datagram
cases.description: Zero bytes. A UDP socket can deliver this.

cases.name: src_push_priority_200_without_expiry
cases.description: The one that matters. A source at priority 200 with flags bit0 clear would sit above the ambient floor forever, and the failure mode has a name: stuck red at 3am. It MUST be rejected at the wire level, so no client can create the condition even by accident, and so a device cannot be talked into it by a buggy controller.
cases.reason: priority 200 above the ambient band with no expiry

cases.name: src_push_priority_64_without_expiry
cases.description: The boundary. The ambient band is 0-63 and is the floor, so 64 is the first priority that must carry an expiry. An implementation that checked for some higher threshold passes the priority-200 case and fails here.
cases.reason: priority 64 is the first above the ambient band

cases.name: src_push_priority_63_without_expiry_is_the_floor
cases.description: The other side of the boundary, and the reason the threshold is 63 rather than 0. An ambient scene at priority 40 with no expiry is not a bug - it is the floor, and a floor that had to expire would not be one. Something has to hold the lights when every show, override and alert has gone. Decode only: this exercises the accept path of the same rule.

cases.name: reserved_bytes_are_ignored_not_rejected
cases.description: An ACTIVATE whose reserved byte is 0xFF. Reserved fields are zero on send and IGNORED on receive; rejecting them would make every future use of that byte a breaking change. Decode only: re-encoding zeroes the byte, which is correct and is why this is not a round-trip case.
cases.reason: reserved fields are never a rejection

cases.name: trailing_bytes_after_a_payload
cases.description: A SYNC_REQ with a ninth payload byte, as a peer one minor version ahead would send after appending a field. Trailing bytes are not an error. Decode only, for the same reason as above.
cases.reason: a newer peer may have appended a field

cases.name: tick_wall_quality_out_of_range
cases.description: wall_quality 4. Unlike a reserved byte this is a defined field with a closed set of values, and guessing at an unknown one would let a schedule fire against a clock nobody vouched for.

cases.name: frame_unknown_pixel_format
cases.description: Pixel format 7. The format decides bytes per pixel, so a decoder that shrugged here would not know where the payload ends.

cases.name: frame_pixel_count_disagrees_with_data
cases.description: count 4 in RGB8 needs twelve pixel bytes; three are present.

cases.name: timectl_unknown_mode
cases.description: mode 9. Acting on an unrecognised time-control mode is how an editor freezes a mesh it cannot then unfreeze.

cases.name: event_kind_is_not_utf8
cases.description: The kind str declares two bytes, 0xFF 0xFE, which are not valid UTF-8. str is defined as UTF-8, so this is a rejection rather than a lossy decode.

cases.name: state_digest_count_exceeds_payload
cases.description: count 3 with one entry present. A decoder that allocated on count before checking the bytes is remotely steerable.

cases.name: prog_begin_string_length_overruns
cases.description: device_class declares 64 bytes with 5 remaining. The length prefix is attacker-controlled and must be checked against what is left, never trusted.
cases.reason: str length 64 exceeds the remaining payload
